utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. I'm sorry for the delay, but I think that the little delay for changing of a bigger courtroom is worth it. Are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've heard on Friday that the -- as you know, there is an ongoing appeal hearing in Krstic. And the Defence in that case as well as the Prosecution would like Mr. Butler to briefly come to their hearing on Wednesday morning to, I believe, just affirm his testimony in this case so that portions of it can be used in that appeal hearing. And I believe the Appellant Chamber has either ordered that or at least has agreed to that. I hope that won't take much time from us. It shouldn't, though you never know who might have questions. I've heard that the Defence don't want to ask questions and I don't think the Prosecution does either. But, as you know, there is an outstanding order from this Chamber that Mr. Butler should not speak to anyone about his testimony. And this, of course, has to do with his testimony, so if we could just loosen that order to include talking potentially to the Defence and the Prosecution in preparation for that testimony, that would be helpful. And I'm sure the Court of Appeals -- I imagine that order doesn't apply to the Court of Appeals, but if it does we should allow them to question him too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In principle I don't have any objections. I would think it would be proper for the meeting to take place while the Defence and the Prosecution are there at the same time. So that way there is no ex parte-ing on either side and then both can communicate to Mr. Butler what it is and come to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Defence. What do you mean by Defence? The Defence in this case are in the Krstic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In the Krstic case. I don't have any -- I have no -- I have nothing to do with that particular case, but I would suspect that if we are going to allow Mr. Butler to have communication with the Prosecution, I would prefer that that communication take place in the presence with the Defence at the same time in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have already discussed this issue, and as far as we are concerned there is no reason for Mr. Butler not to start preparing for cross-examination in the Krstic case. So as far as we are concerned, you have our full cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Sinatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Briefly on that issue, I just wanted to make sure that the Court would allow whatever ample time is taken up in Mr. Stojanovic's cross-examination time that he may be added on Thursday if it runs into his cross-examination, 330-something minutes that the Court has allowed. And I believe the Court will, of course, allow for that if Mr. Butler is not present in the courtroom on Wednesday. But also I'd like to ask this Court's indulgence. We have all filed objections to the intercept evidence motions for the admission of the intercept evidence on November 17th, as ordered by the Trial Chamber. But I would like the indulgence of the Trial Chamber for an extension of time to file our final response to the Prosecution's motion after the final intercept witness who is P -- he's another intercept witness coming as a protected witness, as the last witness listed here before the Christmas holiday. I would like to have the Court's indulgence for an extension of time just a few days after his testimony to file our final objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's deal one matter to another. As to Mr. Butler's testimony on another case, I think this Trial Chamber will allow him to talk to the Prosecution as well as for the Defence. Whether the Defence counsel should be present during the talks with the Prosecution, I don't think it is a matter of this Trial Chamber to decide. I leave it to the Appeals Chamber to decide on this matter. So, Mr. McCloskey, your request is granted. As for the response to Prosecution's submissions concerning the intercept witness, we believe that Ms. Sinatra's request is reasonable, so we could grant you some extension of time for that response, but we have to bear in mind that we have to move fast. So how long do you think, Ms. Sinatra, do you need for that response?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the scheduling goes as planned from the Prosecution's witness list, it seems that witness would testify on December 19th, which is the last day before the Christmas break. If we could have four or five days to file our motion after that time, we would appreciate it, or we would be willing to work out some agreement with the Prosecutor to put that witness up in front of some of the other witnesses that they have listed so that it would not run into the Christmas holidays. Either way, we would like three or four days after the witness testifies to file our final response to the Prosecution's motion for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I will give you five days to file your response whenever this witness is going to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But as I understand the Prosecution's case will be finished after the Christmas recess, maybe in two or three weeks. I hope that we could make the rulings before his case is finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I'm sure that will be possible, Your Honour. We will work expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the time allocated to your case, we'll see the calendar to see whether there's any way out. Thank you. Having said that, could we have the Witness, please. Well, Mr. Karnavas, I got a new list of documents today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's short, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure, I haven't looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can assure you, Mr. President, Your Honours, that I will be finished perhaps even earlier than I had anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. That will make up the time that the Jokic case lost. Well, good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest during the weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For as much as the weather allowed, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll try our best to send you back for Thanksgiving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. But of course, I'm at the disposal of the Court. If you need more time, I'm available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'd like to go back to Mr. Nikolic and discuss that a little bit, kind of nail that down before we move forward. It's my understanding that based on your assessment of the events, that on the night of the 11th to the morning of the 12th, the VRS were under the impression that in all likelihood the 28th Division would be somewhere in the vicinity of the Bandera triangle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, on page 4.384, you testified to that effect. And as I understand it from your testimony, you also state that sweeping operations or sweep operations began, and you used the bulk of the VRS military forces -- began on the morning of the 12th, those sweep operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course when they got there, the 28th Division wasn't there, but nonetheless it would be fair to conclude that the VRS were in that vicinity and therefore some of the units that Mr. Nikolic indicated were at Potocari on the morning of the 12th could not have been there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure of the specific units that he mentioned; however, certainly the elements of the Zvornik Brigade, the Birac Brigade, the 2nd Romanija Brigade were actively sweeping the Bandera triangle on the morning of the 12th, to the best of the knowledge that we have. I don't believe any of the units of the 65 Protection Regiment were involved in that sweep operation. At the same time, again, I have no evidence that they were in Potocari either that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, have you had a chance before coming here today to review his statement of facts and acceptance of responsibility, the one that is dated -- I believe it was introduced as P82 in this case, and it was, I believe, an annex to the plea agreement, and it's dated 6/5/2003. Did you get a chance to look at that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I looked at the day it was signed and finalised. I looked over the entire thing for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you look at it as a matter of curiosity, or was it that they showed it to you in order to get your impression as to whether or not Mr. Nikolic was being accurate and, of course, it would follow, truthful in his rendition of his participation, at least on that -- during the events of -- after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be clear, while that's the first time I saw the document as a package, during the process where he was being interviewed, I was party to meetings afterwards where the Prosecution attorneys would lay out things that he said and ask me to go back and see if it was possible for me to corroborate those issues or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was part of that process and so I think I can answer the questions that are coming up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you, thank you -- I was inching to that, but it would now appear that though you were not inside that room when there were discussions with Mr. Nikolic which we have no tape-recording to see what -- to hear what was said, what was asked and what was answered, it appears now that you would get a debriefing on what he was -- what Mr. Nikolic had said, and thus, they would run it by you to see whether his account would be consistent with or supported by the evidence known by you during the many years of your investigation in this case. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say consistent with. I would -- they would raise issues, and as an issue of credibility they would ask me to go back and see if I was able to corroborate those issues or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. In other words, they would say: Nikolic has told us the following, what do you think? Is there evidence that would support this? Would this be accurate? And so on and so forth, that sort of line of questioning. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would there be any occasions during that period of time when you might suggest a series of questions to the investigator and the Prosecutors that were involved in that process to ask Mr. Nikolic to expound on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And perhaps the best example would be of that was when I was told by the investigator and Mr. McCloskey that Momir Nikolic had -- I don't know if the phrase is taken responsibility, but essentially he told the investigators and the Prosecutor that he was involved in and directed the Kravica warehouse massacre. I understood that from the body of evidence that we had, that there was no evidence which would indicate that. And I did sit down with the Prosecutor and the investigator in question, and we laid out a series of questions that would be useful in trying to determine whether or not he was being truthful in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you think whether those questions were raised, and as a result of those questions that perhaps if we could call it a confrontation, and by that, I mean the form of presenting him with any evidence, that Mr. Nikolic came clean, as it were, or was it that Mr. Nikolic on his own saw the errors of his ways, recognised his sins, and then came forward to confess? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that before we could be confronted on the issue the next day or the next morning, that he in fact had recanted that story. So, to my knowledge -- and, again, I wasn't there, but I have been told that he had recanted prior to being questioned on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So he pre-emptively struck and came up with the truth. But nonetheless you were prepared at that point, you had armed the Prosecution team with the questions and the evidence to confront Mr. Nikolic, because in your opinion, with respect to those events, you were convinced that there was no evidence that could or would support Nikolic's version. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Notwithstanding some of the more colourful statements, I did provide information to the Prosecutor and the investigators that would allow them to question Mr. Nikolic and determine whether he was being truthful on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, as I understand it, on Friday you told us that -- I believe you used the word that there isn't evidence to corroborate that portion of Nikolic's testimony regarding -- that is the issue of the VRS units in Potocari on July 12th and 13th. And this could be found, if you want us to go to it -- could be found on page 72, lines 4 to 5, of the document that we received.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to be clear on that, the units that we're talking about specifically are the 65th Protection Regiment, the Drina Wolves, and the 10th Diversionary. Those are the units we are discussing, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those are the units we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you use the umbrella of VRS, that implies more and that's just why I wanted to bring that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, I want to show you what has been marked as P82 for identification purposes. And if you could look at it. I have an extra copy here if you want to look at it --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to put it on the ELMO, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I don't know whether you like to read it from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually easier reading it off of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could put the extra copy on the ELMO. Now, if I could focus your attention to paragraph number 6, it would be on page 2, it would be at the bottom of it. And it goes -- it runs all the way into the next page by a couple of lines.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this paragraph, we see that he is talking about coordinating with the Drina Wolves, correct, among others -- I'm not going to read everybody, but the Drina Wolves. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The 10th Sabotage Detachment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Elements of the 65th Protection Regiment, the military police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll just focus on that for now. I don't believe we will need the assistance any longer. Thank you. Now, it would seem to me, it would seem to me, that if you were able to identify that, at least with respect to Kravica, Mr. Nikolic was confabulating, potentially, since you have no other evidence that would support that, and since you've told us here that there is no evidence to corroborate the portion of Nikolic's statement, that these particular VRS units, that is, the Drina Wolves of the Zvornik Brigade, the 10th Sabotage Detachment of the Main Staff, and elements of the 65 Protection Regiment military police of the Main Staff, since there was no evidence to corroborate it, did you bring this to the Prosecution's attention and then provide them perhaps with some questions in order to smoke out, if you will, Nikolic in order to provide some verification that indeed these units were in Potocari on the 12th, the morning of the 12th, and that he indeed did in fact coordinate these units among the other units that had been there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this particular respect I do recall raising the issue. The Prosecution is well aware that we have no evidence with respect of these issues. I understand that he was confronted on the general subject of this, and this remains his story. So we -- certainly I understand that there is nothing that could corroborate these parts of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Might I ask why is it that there is nothing -- that no supplemental was prepared by you with respect to perhaps your narration, and there was no mention by you in your direct examination that at least with respect to this portion of Nikolic's testimony, there no evidence to support it. Might I ask why this was never mentioned by you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, as I've indicated a number of times, my narrative is not something where I include the issues of witness testimony. It was, however, discussed. The Prosecution -- you know, obviously we knew Momir Nikolic would be testifying before this Trial Chamber. And the Prosecutor was well aware of the fact that you may well be cross-examining me on issues of Momir Nikolic's credibility. And he knew what I would say in that regard. So I don't know that there's a problem and I don't know that that was something, given the fact that the individual had testified, that was required for me to do on my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- let me take a deep breath at this point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Don't you think it would have been part of your duty as an analyst to point out to the Honourable Members of this Trial Chamber, that at least with respect to the star witness of the Prosecution on this particular issue with respect to coordination, which was hotly contested during the cross-examination of Mr. Nikolic, that you had a duty, a fundamental duty, to come forward and say: With respect to this portion of Nikolic's testimony, I cannot find any corroborating evidence. Don't you think that you had that duty?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't. And if that, in fact, is going to be an implied duty, we might be here an awful long time as I go through each and every witness determining where I can and cannot corroborate their story. Again, the purpose of my being forward as an analyst for the Office of the Prosecutor in this respect is to provide context behind the documents and the intercepts, not to pass value judgements as to whether or not I believe or whether or not I can corroborate witnesses who have testified before the Trial Chamber. Obviously when I'm asked that question, I will offer an opinion, but that is not something that is envisioned by me as a primary duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip forward a little bit. I wasn't going to get there until the end, but I think I'm just going to have to get there a little bit sooner just for the point of raising it. On Friday, sir, we heard a speech by you with respect to how conservative and fair-minded you were, this can be found on page 30 to 31, line 16 to line 5. Now you indicated, as you said, that as a military man you had more in common with the accused here and therefore you wanted to be, and you strive to be, conservative and fair in analysing documents. Can we not conclude from that little statement of yours that by that which is -- what you were trying to tell us is that when in doubt, the doubt would -- the accused would have the benefit of it, when in doubt in analysing documents. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would analyse them as conservatively as possible, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you not think that you as an analyst, the fact that you have been working on this case for five to six years, the fact that you have questioned many, many witnesses in the field, the fact that you've had at your disposal all of the evidence, all of the disclosure material that has been available to the Prosecution, the fact that you have been sitting and strategising with the Prosecution, do you think that providing that information openly, fairly, reasonably to this Tribunal would have been - not to the Defence, but at least to the Tribunal - would have been necessary as part of your duty to provide exculpatory information, not merely inculpatory information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, the question is with respect to -- is it my obligation to go through Prosecution witnesses and witness statements, highlighting the issues where I can either corroborate their story or I believe they're being untruthful, and that as a component of my Rule 68, pass them to Defence, or basically pass them to the Prosecution to pass to Defence. That's the question, I believe, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the question, but also a component of that question is in informing the Honourable Members of this Trial Chamber, that with respect to this portion of the testimony on a hotly contested issue, because we've been talking about whose responsibility these people -- these prisoners and refugees were, do you not think you had an obligation to say: However, there is one portion of the testimony of Momir Nikolic, a portion that was in his statement of facts and his acceptance of responsibility, that I as an analyst cannot and will not adopt because there is no evidence to corroborate that portion of his testimony. Do you not think you had an obligation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. There is -- Mr. Butler is under no duty to adopt Mr. Nikolic's testimony, which his counsel is suggesting by his question. This is getting into repetition upon repetition, and it's becoming argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, I understand that your question has a point, but it's really a repetitive question. You have asked this question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not getting a sufficient answer; that's the problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It does. It does. Trial and error, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- I don't want to move on too far off this subject before I cover one other point. Did you get a chance, did you get a chance, to listen to the Prosecutor's statement during Nikolic's sentencing hearing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, with respect to this particular issue, he states, and I quote, it's on day -- it's on page -- I can provide a copy to everyone. It's on page 18, if we could have it. If we could put -- if you could locate -- it's kind of hard to find the pages, but if you could go to page, I believe it would be 18, page 18. And I'll read from line 2. It states: "The task of understanding Potocari, what happened there, the units that were involved, is made so much clearer by Mr. Nikolic's testimony because we know what happened. We know from the" -- and then it goes on. Now, this portion of that statement would seem to contradict what you've indicated to us, and that is that it's not made clearer because certain portions of Mr. Nikolic's testimony with respect to the units involved in Potocari on that particular day, there is no evidence to corroborate it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. There is no evidence to corroborate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's not made clearer, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is or not. That will be up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I understand that in many cases Mr. Nikolic's statement and testimony certainly isn't as complete as I would personally like to see it, and it is my understanding that at the end of the day with Mr. Nikolic that the Prosecutor is only going to ask the Court to believe that which we can corroborate for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So how much or how little clearer it gets is a very subjective opinion, sir, and I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you -- I'm going to move on. I'll resist asking that question. Then if we go on to line 8 and 9, and Mr. McCloskey --: "We now know without a shadow of a doubt what happened there. This is very valuable." Now, we don't know without a shadow of a doubt what happened there, at least not as a result of Mr. Nikolic's testimony, because as you indicated there is no evidence to corroborate his version of the events that he -- that certain VRS units were there, and that he was coordinating them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're going to put me on trial, can we have the entire statement put in evidence, and I don't understand the relevance of this. I know particularly what I meant. It's being taken out of context, and I don't really understand the relevance of taking argument by counsel. And if it's going to be allowed, the entire context should be allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree -- totally agree with Mr. McCloskey. I would move to have the entire statement from the sentencing hearing moved into the record for this particular case, Your Honour. I 100 per cent absolutely agree with that. And my intention is not to take anything out of context, but merely to point out: Here is an instance where perhaps there was an obligation on the part of the Prosecution to at least point out that there might be some problems with Mr. Nikolic, as opposed to adopting it, which in fact shows that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't see the linkage between putting me on trial and a duty. We have not been able to corroborate everything that Mr. Nikolic has said. That's very clear. We can't corroborate everything all our witnesses have said. That's very clear. Mr. Butler can certainly be cross-examined on all those points. But putting a counsel's statement at a sentencing hearing into evidence is certainly not relevant. And if counsel thinks it's relevant, fine. I have a lot I can say on that point, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I think you have already made your point. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm moving on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you not submit this opening statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if the Court does not wish to have it, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because is point is very clear here in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: There is no need for you to submit it into the evidence, this is first. Secondly, well, it's a very rare practice to put an opening statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But while I'm still with Mr. Nikolic, one other issue that I think we need no cover with respect to this, this issue of the units. He also talks that there were units, VRS, military police units over there, does he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Drina Corps, he says corps military units, and then also he talks about MUP being over there, and specifically Mr. Jevic, Stalin aka Stalin?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it would seem to me, if we follow the reasoning, that if there's no evidence to corroborate that at least some of those units were there, we might be able to say that there is no evidence to corroborate that Mr. Nikolic ever received any orders from Colonel Jankovic on the morning of the 12th while he was in front of the Hotel Fontana to go and coordinate certain units. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is again argument for the credibility of Mr. Nikolic, which is the Court's -- it's the Court's duty. It is a fine argument to make, but this is not relevant to this Witness. If he has particular facts, figures, documents, fine, but this is a credibility argument, which is a fine credibility argument, but there is not the proper witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But we believe Mr. Karnavas has the might to make sure which units were present at that time. Maybe you could put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. According to Mr. Nikolic, there are units there from the Main Staff. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There are units there from the corps. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He says that there are units there from the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then he also says that there are civilian units from MUP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we know, do we not, that Momir Nikolic is a captain in the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we talked a little bit on Friday about a couple of concepts regarding the unity of command and function of relationships. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Jankovic is with the Main Staff, is he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it you've had an opportunity to read Mr. Nikolic's statement of facts and also to read his testimony when he testified in this case, have you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the issue of Colonel Jankovic, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it would seem to me -- well, here is a captain of a brigade being ordered by the Main Staff to go and coordinate, issue orders to a certain extent, to higher echelon units, is he not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, that certainly is not in keeping with the principle of unity of command, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would you not also agree with me that it's not even -- it's not in keeping with the concept of functional relationships as we understand it and as we analyse it in accordance with the rules?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So did that bother you at all? When you read that, did you scratch your head a little bit and say, you know, something just doesn't seem right. How could this captain, not even first class, in their terms - that is, first class in ours - how could he be given an oral task to go to Potocari and to give orders to higher-echelon officers from the Main Staff and the Drina Corps as well as MUP? How is that possible? Did it raise a red flag, as they say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two questions here, so let me answer them in turn. The first question is: Yes, I was -- it did raise at least a professional interest on my part with this respect. And the problem, of course, that I have is I have no information that would confirm or deny this. There's nothing in the documents or the intercepts which would allow me to corroborate that portion of his story. As to the second question, the only way I believe that the relationships or the order process that you described can occur, is if the fact that all of the commanders in question had been informed exactly what the plan would be and that Captain Nikolic, Captain First Class Nikolic would be the person who would be coordinating to make sure that all the actions worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But like I said, going back to the first part of your question which I think is the most important part of it, is that I have no evidence one way or another that could confirm or deny that series of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go back -- I want to go to the second part of your answer, because you said that they would have to have a meeting, they would have to know that Nikolic is in charge. Can we also throw into the mix that it would be incumbent upon Mr. Nikolic to also know what each of these units was tasked to do?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, for that to work, he would have to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we don't find that in his testimony, do we, that he actually knew what they had been tasked to do. We don't find that. Do you recall reading that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If it were in the transcript, and I can dig it up, and if it were and you're willing to trust me that it is in the transcript, would that give you some further pause as to perhaps what Nikolic is telling us, given his rank and given the fact that we know that there is no evidence with respect to some of the units and all the other things that we know was happening, can we reach some kind of conclusion that in all probability, perhaps even a very high probability, that what Mr. Nikolic is telling us about his role as a coordinator in Potocari is unsubstantiated by the weight of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of his role as a coordinator is unsubstantiated with respect to the documents and the intercepts. Whether or not substantiation is derived by the video or what little video evidence we have of that is an open question; my opinion is that it is not. We know that there are some events that occurred prior that, for example, at 8.00 in the morning on the 12th, there was a meeting between Mladic, Krstic, presumably other army principals, and representatives of the MUP. And we don't know all of the details that were discussed at that meeting. So we are dealing with a lot of unknowns, and because of that we don't have the ability -- or certainly I don't have the ability to corroborate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you would agree with me that the task of coordinating all of these particular units, given the events on the ground, was rather a significant role, a significant task. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And does it not trouble you that not only do we not have any corroborating evidence, but Mr. Nikolic indicates that he is told of this order, or he's given this order by Jankovic orally outside the Hotel Fontana. Doesn't that piece of evidence, piece of his testimony, doesn't that give you pause into thinking that perhaps Mr. Nikolic is confabulating here also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is a massive misstatement of the evidence. There is tremendous amount of evidence on the record. I won't go into it all, but Mr. Nikolic was coordinating from the DutchBat, from the Muslims, from the Serbs that have testified. For Mr. Karnavas to say there is no support that he was coordinating is absolutely absurd and a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe that the Witness already told us that he has no evidence to confirm that piece of the evidence. Also, there is no evidence for him to deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think it could get very far on that point, but your point has already been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will no respond to the Prosecution and I don't want the record to reflect that I'm acquiescing to his account to his objection. The fact that I'm -- I just want to save time and move on, so rather than argue the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't we move on to another topic. Let's talk about the Cerska incident. And as I recollect your testimony on this particular case, you had indicated to us that this was perhaps the -- that you had an intercept that you believed specifically related to the beginning of the organised mass execution process. Do you recall stating that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that the Cerska Valley execution was the first visible manifestation of the organised mass execution process, and we have two intercepts several hours apart, which I believe are related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me show you now a portion of your testimony, just so you have it handy there. It's pages -- we'll start with page 4463. It dates Thursday, 13 November 2003. I'm not going to read it all, so there's no need to get alarmed. But you will see from page 3 -- do we have one for the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can put this one on the ELMO, sir, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have an extra one for the ELMO. We will see that you're being shown Exhibit 208 and it states there that there is an intercept, I believe, dated on the 13th, and it reflects that it was 1355, which would mean 5 minutes before 2.00 in the afternoon. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe this is the exhibit that you're telling us is the first intercept that at least -- it's the first indication or is indicative of the beginning of the organised mass execution process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is related to it, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in this particular intercept, you noted that it was Colonel Milanovic who was making an inquiry from Palma regarding the availability of a bulldozer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was making it to Palma.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To Palma, right, regarding the availability of a bulldozer. Right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, or bucket loader, or earth-moving machine. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then you indicate that this particular piece of corresponds, corresponds, I'm underscoring that, to the testimony you believe is before the Court with respect to the mass execution which occurred in the Cerska Valley area at approximately 1.00 on the 13th, 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now here you say 1.00, 1300. Now, I would like to show you a portion of the transcript where the particular witness testified in the Krstic case. And I'm referring to page 2737; it's dated Wednesday, 12 April 2000. The witness is identified as Witness M.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And -- now, do you recall seeing this at any particular point in time, seeing this or being aware of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the testimony I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, it says -- he says that it was the 13th of July. And then he says on line 3: "It was about 2.00 in the afternoon and I noticed trucks and buses passing by, moving from Konjevic Polje towards Nova Kasaba." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is -- just to stop there before we go any further, that would be slightly different from the 1300 hours that you have. This is 1400 hours that he's talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm one hour off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're one hour off, although we know from the intercept that you referred to earlier, Exhibit 208, that that is 1355, which is closer to, at least this point in time when the gentleman indicates that he sees buses passing by moving towards Konjevic Polje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then he describes who he was with and that at some point the buses, the two buses, you know, took a turn off the asphalt road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then that -- further down he indicates that there was an APC following them. And that on line 18 he says: "Maybe five or ten minutes after that, a yellow backhoe started out in the same direction and I could watch it travel as well and at that point, we could only hear fire of small firearms." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if we were to analyse this and maybe synthesise it, it would appear that based on the gentleman's testimony back on 12 April 2000, it is his recollection that it was approximately 2.00 and that sometime after five or ten minutes of seeing the buses, which would place it somewhere around 2.05, 2.10, 2.15, maybe slightly later, 2.20, whatever, somewhere around that vicinity, but no more than five or ten minutes after seeing the buses is when he sees the backhoe. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here we have, here we have, at least with Exhibit 202, we have Milanovic, Colonel Milanovic asking, asking for a bulldozer just about the same time that this gentleman sees the buses veer off. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, how far is Palma duty station to Konjevic Polje or to this area, to this area where they need to get the bulldozer to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly 15 to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And how long would it take, how long would it take, given the conditions of the road, what was happening, and the speed that one of these vehicles would travel, how long would it take for them to get to that location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the problem, sir. I don't know the speed that they would travel, so I couldn't speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I will -- give or take an hour, an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I take it since you're speculating with us, and I don't have any reasons to doubt that you're in a ballpark figure, this was a question that was never asked.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The one that I just asked you: How long would it take for a bulldozer to get from point A to point B, in other words from the Palma area where the request is being made to the area where the buses have veered off.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that is correct, because with the intercept indicating that the equipment was not available, that kind of negated a path of investigation which would be how long to get from point A to point B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would it be fair to say that at least with respect to these two -- with what we've just seen, that it's not quite as clear as you may imply it to be, in other words here we are five minutes before 2.00 a request is made. 2.00 a gentleman sees the buses. Five to ten minutes later he sees the backhoe. Would you say that there is a disconnect with respect to these two pieces of evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say there is a disconnect at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you indicated, you indicated, that there was another piece of evidence, another intercept, that further assisted you - and I believe it might be on another page - that further assisted you in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's back to P459.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: P45 -- right -- well, hold on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the portion of the transcript you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at the transcript, I believe it's P211.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On the transcript we see it's page 4466.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have it up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And here we have the same gentleman, Colonel Milanovic, making a request - this is on P211 - for an excavator or a bulldozer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And now the time, now the time, is 1553. So that would be around 3.53 in the afternoon. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Close to two hours, close to two hours, after the initial request and after the gentleman who had been the eyewitness to this event says that he saw the truck -- the buses veer off the road. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yet it would appear, would it not, that Colonel Milanovic is still looking for that bulldozer or excavator that he had requested two hours earlier. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so it would appear -- now, if we take this into consideration, this piece of evidence into consideration, along with the eyewitness account, assuming that that is accurate, in other words that the date is accurate -- and incidentally we have no corroborating evidence that that date is accurate - that is the 13th - that perhaps he didn't see it on the 14th or the 15th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. What the witness says is what he says, and we can't corroborate that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact when the bodies were exhumed from those graves, there was no way to corroborate what exactly, the exact date that they had been killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the exhumation process, that's correct. I'm -- I seem to recall that there were additional witness statements which indicate people passing over that grave site, which they may have used as a way to time when the grave was installed. So I'm unclear on that but I think there is some other information with respect to when we believe the grave was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I guess what I'm getting at, there is a possibility, given that we don't have any other evidence, other than this gentleman's testimony, that the date could have been the 14th as opposed to the 13th or the 15th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is that possibility, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at, if we look at, these two intercepts plus the gentleman's testimony, it would seem that it raises some questions, does it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I guess what I'm asking is: It would appear that you may wish to somewhat qualify your earlier position and that this particular intercept, the one that I first showed you which was P208, is really not as conclusive in determining, in determining, the beginning of the organised mass execution process. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know understand what you mean by conclusive. My comment was that this is the first piece of evidence that we have, notwithstanding witness testimony, of the beginning of the mass execution process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, assuming, assuming, because that's why I asked you, is it possible that this gentleman was wrong, since we don't have any corroborating evidence, that this gentleman was wrong and the execution actually took place on the 14th, then would it not follow that this incident would not have been the beginning of the organised mass execution process, and perhaps another incident further down in time or maybe even earlier might have been the beginning of the organised mass execution process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's two pieces to that. First, working on your assumption and perhaps where maybe there's some confusion in correlating the two, I never assumed that with respect to the particular witness that the one piece of earth-moving equipment that he described was the only one that everyone was looking for. The general pattern with the grave sites that we have is that it was multiple pieces of equipment. So I always hold open the possibility -- and I believe it is exactly what had happened in this case is that they were looking for additional equipment because they needed more for the grave. Now, for your second piece, clearly if the witness is mistaken on the date and it is, in fact, the 14th or the - excuse me - or the 15th, then certainly you're correct, that wouldn't be the first manifestation of the mass execution process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I guess the bottom line is at this point in time is that there is insufficient evidence to make a -- to form a conclusion as to whether it happened on the 13th or the 14th or the 15th or even as late as the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, that is a legal argument calling for a legal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you finish that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have -- it may get a little messy, so we'll save it for after the break. I'll regroup so I can streamline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll have a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, we were on the Cerska incident when we left off, and we were discussing the issue of this -- of these two intercepts where Colonel Milanovic is asking for a bulldozer. Now, were you aware of that the Prosecution brought forward a witness who goes by P140? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number in abstract doesn't mean anything to me. I would have to have a bit of a description of the witness of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're like me. This was a gentleman that apparently was asked to participate in the burying of the bodies in Glogova on the 11th and the 12th -- or the 12th and the 13th. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, now I know who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact he indicated sometime in the middle of the night on the 13th, someone whom he believed was from Sarajevo because of the accent came and asked him to go to Kravica, but it wasn't until the following day that he set off. That's the same person that we're talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, he had indicated that he spent the -- those -- I believe it was the 12th, 13th or the 11th, 12th, and 13th, one, first burying the bodies of the Serb soldiers, and then secondly, I believe it was for the 12th and 13th, he was burying bodies who he thought were -- had been out there decomposing for three or four days. And these would have been bodies of Muslim soldiers or Muslim men. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is his testimony, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And given where -- and I believe in Glogova where he was doing this sort of work at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- with respect to burying the bodies of the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he says that he started creating the grave -- I want to be sure on this one. I believe he says he started creating the grave on the 13th, and then he was -- he started creating the open -- the hole on the 13th and then he was taken to the warehouse on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I don't want to misstate his evidence, obviously. I think that's the way it was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, his testimony was on page -- with respect to this particular issue goes from page 3.407 and it's not until 3.418 that he indicates that the bodies that he was asked to bury on that particular day or days seemed to him to be about three or four days decomposing and infection was spreading, so he had to bury them as soon as possible. And this could be found on lines 6 to 8. My question, however, is this: In light of this activity, is it possible, and in light of what we know from this gentleman who was called by the Prosecution and of course his account that these bodies had been out there for three or four days, or as much as three or four days and that they were decomposing and infection was spreading, is it possible or is it not possible that Colonel Milanovic might have been calling for a bulldozer to assist this particular gentleman with that particular task. Is that not within the range of possibilities, particularly since we have him making a request at 2.00 in the afternoon, or five minutes to 2.00, and then again two hours later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe it is because I don't think that the timing issue works. I could explain that in detail, if you want, but I just don't think the timing synchronises on that. Again, the problem is, to our knowledge, significant -- where you would find bodies of Bosnian Muslims on those early days. Certainly there were bodies of Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica town on the 11th and 12th. There would be presumably some in and around Potocari. The column did not start to come into significant contact until the 12th and 13th. The only bodies that were showing up on the road where they could be retrieved were those from later on in the afternoon of the 13th, at least according to what the witnesses have testified to. So other than Bosnian Muslims who had been killed in Potocari, I don't know of another group. My understanding is they didn't start removing the dead bodies out of Srebrenica until almost the 15th or 16th. That's the problem I have. I just don't think the timing of where we have large groups of bodies synchronises with that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now are you making any particular conclusion as to whether this gentleman, or witness P140 called by the Prosecution was being truthful on this particular matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he's truthful or not, it's not for me to say. However, I've had some issues with respect to what he's testified. And for example, to my knowledge no soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade were killed with respect to the takedown of Srebrenica. The question that raises in my mind is that who is he burying on 12 July 1995, because my understanding of the customs at the time were if soldiers from other units were going to be buried, they would be brought to their home villages and buried there. They would not be buried in Bratunac. So there are a lot of issues that raise questions with me, and one of the things that I always do have to try and keep into account is that many of these people are recalling events that occurred five and six years ago, and there may be day-off periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, earlier there was one question I asked you and you made a -- you took a stab at it, and that was with respect to how long it would take the bulldozer to go from the Palma area to where it was being requested by Colonel Milanovic, and I believe you said an hour and a half, an hour to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that's a wheeled one. I mean, it may be the same. I don't know what it would take if it was a tracked one. They would probably obviously want to put it on a flatbed, rather than run it on its tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for comparative purposes, if I could -- the gentleman here, P140, I can provide you with the statement or I can just read it into the record, lines 4 to 7, he stated: "It would have taken us," meaning him and his colleague, "at least one and a half hours, up to two hours, to reach Kravica," that is, from where -- from Bratunac to Kravica that's where he's talking about. Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's crawling on tracks on its own power, that's probably reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree with me that between Bratunac and Kravica, the distance is much shorter, or shorter, than between -- the area where Colonel Milanovic is requesting these bulldozers to come to from Palma?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How much of a difference would that be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably about 14 kilometres. I'm thinking it's about 9 from Bratunac to Kravica, it may be less. I said 20, so probably -- certainly 10 to 15. Let's put it in a ballpark range there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if it would take one to one and a half -- one and a half hours up to two hours from Bratunac to Kravica, would it take perhaps anywhere from three to four hours if it was coming from Palma all the way to where it was being requested by Colonel Milanovic? Would that be a fair estimation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Karnavas, the unknown variable is, one, whether we're talking a wheeled vehicle. And they did have wheeled engineer equipment. If we're talking a tracked vehicle, that would be a fair one. If it was a tracked vehicle that came on a flatbed, it might not be valid. So it is all dependent upon the vehicle and the mode by which they want to do it by. That's why I was always reluctant to do that. There are too many variables in your equation to make an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we could move to another subject. I want to talk to you a little bit about Kravica. Now, you've testified with respect to Kravica and you have indicated that it's your understanding that the incident that occurred there would have taken place sometime around 5.00 in the afternoon. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is what the witness accounts, or the survivor accounts in this instance claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that survivor singular or is that survivors plural?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's the two survivors, and I believe the range, time, that they give is between 1600 and 1800.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could show you, just so we can have some precision here, a thing that we strive for in this courtroom, page 4483 of the transcript. If I could give that to you. I if could have the assistance of Madam Usher. Thank you. And this was an Thursday, 13 November 2003. Just for contextual purposes, on line 20 to 21, you were asked about a particular exhibit, Exhibit 220. Do you -- Mr. Butler, if you would like to have an extra copy, we have one here for your convenience.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So here you're asked about Exhibit 220, and then you begin to answer that it's a conversation between Krstic and Borovcanin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go into the next page -- that was just for context. If we go on to the next page, you are asked, you are asked - and this would be page 4484 of the record - you're asked a question on line 17 and it states: "And at 2040 hours on 13 July, would that have been anywhere here the time the Kravica warehouse killings?" And you answer, same page, line 19: "This conversation would be occurring approximately three hours, three and a half hours from the beginning of the executions. And if survivor accounts are accurate, approximately an hour after the last of the series of shootings." Now, do you recall giving us that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if we were to work it backwards, then it would appear that your understanding is based on at least the testimony of one of the survivors, correct, as far as when the shooting began?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony is based on what I believe both of the survivors, or the range that they give, as well as the -- I believe there is a time hack on the Borovcanin video as well as the corresponding records from the Bratunac centre, which show people who were there at approximately that time. So I believe -- that's what I'm hinging my 1700 time on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now if I could show you a part of the transcript with respect to Witness P106 who testified in this courtroom. Thank you, Madam Usher. I apologise for having you walk back and forth. And actually what I've handed you starts with page 1243, it's Monday, 14 July 2003. And actually I've given you more than enough. But if we could turn to page 1245. Now I'm cross-examining here the individual, and I state, question, line 12: "And it's my understanding that you've described the shooting taking place from 5.00 in the afternoon." "A. In my opinion, it was about that time, perhaps it was later, perhaps it was earlier, but I think it was about 5.00." I then go down -- I then ask a question on line 20: "Okay. Now, as I indicated, there's another individual who was there at the time that you were there, and he's given a statement and has indicated that: 'There was an earlier incident that occurred outside the warehouse, sometime perhaps around 5.00 or so - it's unclear - and that the shooting, the actual shooting took place at around 9.00 at night or 10.00, when it was dark.'" And then I ask: "My question is: Do you recall any shooting taking place?" The answer is: "No, it wasn't. The shooting started before night fell. It starred before dark and continued until night fell." And then I tried to pin the gentleman down. There's some objections, and I move on. Now, sir, did you have an opportunity to be acquainted with this portion of the testimony that came into this courtroom before you coming here to testify?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me provide you what has been marked for identification purposes as D11. I believe this may already have been introduced by the Defence, and if I could show you this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could -- are we back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we were to turn our attention to page 6, sir, page 6. And I believe we can put this safely on the ELMO because there are no names. There are some initials, but I don't think that would compromise anything at the bottom of the page. If we were to go there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could - I'm sorry - keep the initials off the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I have no problem. I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, I don't need the last paragraph. What I do need is the paragraph before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we may fold that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just need the part that says -- the paragraph that starts with: "Before the execution."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay we're fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I believe it might be relevant for all of us here if I -- if we would just go through the entire paragraph, though the specific part that I'm looking for is only three or four lines, but it gives a slightly different account. Now, this particular witness indicates, and I read on page 6 of his statement taken by the Office of the Prosecution. And this was on -- I can't see the date here, but in any event it says: "Before the execution actually started as reported in the statement I gave in 1996, the following event happened. All of a sudden, explosions started very nearby while the soldiers were still inside the warehouse. The blasts were close and I heard a tyre of a bus leaking air with a very characteristic noise. A lot of automatic fire was to be heard and from the opening I saw a Chetnik firing in direction of the woods. I could also hear a nearby tank and anti-aircraft gun shooting. The Serb soldiers were shouting that they were attacked by our people but I don't understand how this could have been possible since our people had no weapons with them which could fire grenades. Once this first wave of fire calmed a bit, the soldiers ordered two prisoners to get out in order to help collect alleged Serb soldiers which got wounded. They went out for less than a minute and returned. They did that a few times, running out and then returning inside. They did not tell what they saw outside. The shooting then became sporadic for a while. Once the shooting stopped, the soldier with a blue helmet who was guarding at gunpoint wanted to shoot at us, but one younger soldier did prevent him to shoot. I did not understand what was happening. The soldiers were shouting at us saying "We have opened a corridor for your people to get out and look what they do to us." After that, the soldiers were then standing next to the entrance getting in and out and about a half an hour later, when it was getting dark, so I assume around 1100 hours these soldiers --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, that's 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or 21, I'm sorry. I apologise. That would be 9.00 p.m.. "These soldiers who were guarding us started to open fire at us from the entrance without any apparent reason." Now, do you recall ever reading this portion of one of the survivors' statements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, that it is different in time as the account of the other survivor, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact this would place the shooting to have taken place, that is the shooting that -- the atrocity itself, sometime on or about 9.00 p.m. at night. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he says it was getting dark. We know that time of year, the days seem to be slightly longer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So his account, at least to when the shooting would have taken place, would be consistent with the -- what we all know are the hours, the daylight hours during that period of the year. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, yeah, with 2100 hours would be getting dark. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he seems to indicate that perhaps prior to this incident -- in fact, several hours before this incident that there was an earlier incident outside, which was smaller, much smaller. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He indicates it was a shooting incident earlier, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Which also might be consistent with what we now know -- the incident that occurred where a Muslim prisoner got a hold of a weapon and shot and killed one of the Serb soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is a -- there is speculation to that effect, but I don't think that fairly can be interpreted and something we know as a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour, I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We do have information, do we not, that reflects that sometime earlier -- sometime during that afternoon, a Muslim soldier was able to get a hold of a weapon from one of the Serb soldiers and was able to kill one of the Serb soldiers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data that we have indicates that one of the Serb soldiers, and to be specific, he is a member of the Sekovici Special Police Brigade -- or the 2nd Sekovici detachment - was killed at 1700 hours. In various interviews with some of the Bosnian Serbs, they recount the story that that is in fact how he died. A Bosnian Muslim did come out and attempt to take his weapon and in fact shoot him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, not that a Muslim soldier came out, but rather as I recall it, and correct me if I'm wrong, that this particular individual wanted to make some inquiries with respect to how one of his relatives had been killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may very well be, but I just don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless, nonetheless, at least we have some accounts from Serbs, Serb soldiers, that would in some way with consistent with a portion of this gentleman's testimony that we just read, that an incident had occurred sometime at or around 5.00 or 5.30. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that this gentleman's statement - and that is reflected in D11 - is indeed slightly different with respect to the timing of the atrocity to the other survivor who testified as a Prosecution witness in this case as P106. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There would be a discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And it would appear that given that we have these two divergent statements and given your account as you gave it on 13 November 2003, you made a preference. Correct?
