I believe one of the vehicles again listed from Birac Holding, and we have references of a BGH-700, from which I don't know where it originated from, although the -- it was also apparently in Orahovac and it was moved on the 17th from Orahovac to Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that in the burial operations in Branjevo, there were also elements of the civilian protections of Zvornik municipality and the R Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of members of the R Battalion, as well as some incidents of, perhaps, the 1st Battalion moving bodies from Pilica Dom to Branjevo. I don't believe I've heard of elements of civilian protection in Zvornik with -- associated with the burial at Branjevo. That doesn't sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who participated in the burial operations in Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have no specific records which would indicate which actual pieces of equipment were involved in Petkovci. Again, all we have in this regard is the notation from the engineer company's workbook that pieces of equipment were there digging graves -- or working at the dam, actually. Going over the documents which reflect the engineer equipment used, none of them reflect work at Petkovci on either the 15th or 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any members of military formations in Petkovci? If so, do you know which formations those were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The formation in question in Petkovci would be the 6th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. And with respect to the 6th Infantry Battalion, we do have vehicle records which note a series of trips on 15 July 1995 to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then conclude that members of the 6th Battalion did indeed participate in the burial of the bodies there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect their activity involved the movement of numbers of bodies from the school at Petkovci to the dam. I don't know whether -- I mean, we have that from some -- from the documents or the records in that respect. I don't know if they were actually present with respect to the actual excavation of the burial site at the foot of the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then agree that the process of burial also implied this segment, the transport of the bodies from Branjevo and from Pilica to the site of burial and in part Petkovci -- the transport from the school to the place where they were buried in Petkovci. Would that also be involved in this whole thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that would be a fair statement. We know that from witnesses that at least of the detention sites, Orahovac, Petkovci, and the school at Kula, that there were various numbers of Bosnian Muslims who were killed in those facilities. So while the bulk of the people executed did so or died on the killing fields, so to speak, there were bodies at each of the schools, which presumably would have to be policed up and brought to the burial site itself. In the case of Pilica Dom, or the dome of culture in that respect, all of those bodies would have to have been brought from the Dom to the Branjevo Military Farm where they were buried with the other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can the chief of engineering, in view of his authority, ever direct elements of a battalion and can the chief of engineering direct the commander of an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Within his competence, the chief of engineering directs the activities of the engineer company. He does not have the competence to give orders to infantry battalion commanders unless specifically directed to do so by the chief of staff or brigade commander in that instance. That is not something he would do as a normal basis of his functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. This is what I wanted to get in the answer. Can the chief of engineering, as a rule, direct - again the term "direction" - direct the utility company or direct the civilian protection units?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the utility company, my understanding is that the assistant commander for rear services would be the most logical focal point or individual to do the interface and coordination between the military logistics branch and the civilian economic infrastructure. With respect to civilian protection units, I suspect that that would be something that would be -- that would have to be coordinated by the brigade commander or chief of staff. They may choose to do it through the assistant commander for rear services, but I do not believe that within his competence that assistant commander can independently direct those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, it's obvious that the chief of engineering in any situation cannot be the one to direct any of these assets.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I mean, certainly the chief of engineering would be the person who would have the largest or the most comprehensive background on the general availability of civilian engineering assets which might have military uses. But according to the rules, the procedure should be that once those assets have been identified as being required for requisition by the military, the requisition process would go through the assistant commander for rear services.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Butler. We are prepared to also show how this works in practice, but we'll come to that. As far as I have understood you, direction, according to the instructions on the work of commands and staff, implies planning, organising, commanding, coordination, and control. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe using the phrase "direction," yes those are all part of the overall process by which a -- I don't want to say just a commander, but a person in charge at the superior level enforces his tasks or directions on subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So am I right when I say that the term "direction," the chief of engineering cannot be the person or cannot be at the level strategic, operative, or tactical which would be able to plan, oversee, organise, and execute a certain activity in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree. I would say that with respect to the brigade that his responsibility as the chief of engineering, it is within his competence to be able to plan engineer operations. And at the -- he recommends them to the commander or chief of staff. Once these recommendations are accepted, he then works on behalf of the commander or chief of staff to oversee them, to ensure they're organised properly, and if necessary give supplemental orders in order to ensure that the task is carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the work and the analysis of what happened in the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th of July, did you come across any written document which implied planning of these activities and which was signed by the chief of engineering, Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to orders or things of that nature, I do not have any orders signed by Dragan Jokic as the chief of engineering during that 14th through 17th July period. So in that respect, I do not have documents which would manifest such a planning process.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you come to any knowledge about there being a written document in the form of a travel or a work authorisation conducive to sending the mechanical equipment to Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't have a document which reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I think that you've also said that when you -- in your testimony -- so I just wanted to continue. In the course of your analysis of the evidence that was available to you, did you ever come across information that Dragan Jokic was physically present at any one of those burial sites that we mentioned, Orahovac, Petkovci, Kozluk, and Branjevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe that I have come across any evidence which physically puts him -- during the periods that the burial operation took place, from the 14th through the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, for that answer. And another question from this particular area and then I will be finished with it. I understood, and I learned today, that the elements of command, the instruments, documents of command, orders, commands, instructions, and directives. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe those definitions come out of the manual for the work of command and staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your analysis, did you ever come across any document in this period - we're talking about the whole period of July 1995 - in the form of an order, a command, an instruction, or a directive which was signed by Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that we have one of those, sir, no, during this period of July 1995. There may be some towards the back end of the month that we haven't examined, but certainly from the period to 23 July 1995, other than, for example, the duty book that we've received recently from Colonel Obrenovic, there are no orders or other documents that are signed by, at that time, Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Butler. Although I asked whether there was an order, a command, an instruction, and a directive, so the notes in this book are not in the form or are not the contents of an order. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that same respect, so then the answer would be: No, there are no documents that I am aware of that reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come to that book, and we will analyse each note that is written down in that book, but let's continue. Could you please help me, in order to clarify certain practical situations which occurred in that period, on the 14th and the 15th. Could you please tell me what the term "resubordination" means, what does it imply?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term implies or defines the act where a unit or formation which is normally organic to one formation or its parent formation is - and I don't want to mix terms of art here, but it is attached to another unit for either a specific time or specific tasks. I don't want to mix, again, Western term of art and JNA, but it essentially is the taking of a unit from where it normally belongs and then putting it under the command of a different unit in order to conduct its military tasks. It is temporary in nature; it is not considered to be a permanent type of change.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the unit is placed under the command of another unit. Under the term "command," does that imply control of the legality of the execution of the combat tasks of this subordinated unit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the -- the way it was to be defined within the JNA and later VRS, it would with respect to not only the execution of the combat tasks but -- and also a wider role with respect to other issues. For example, in a Western term of art with respect to this, attached or put under the operational control of one unit is a limiting term which means for the use in combat tasks or other tasks that have been agreed to. Within the VRS, as I understand it as it was exercised in 1995, it could be broader. For example, if a soldier in a unit that had been resubordinated from one command to another had committed a criminal act, under their doctrine it would be the responsibility of the unit command which he had been resubordinated to to initiate the procedure for criminal sanctions. That's different than in the Western system where it normally would still be the responsibility of the parent command or the original command to do that. In other areas, for example, such as personnel administration, while the unit is resubordinated for combat tasks, the parent unit still maintains responsibility for personnel administration of the soldiers or officers with respect to pay, with respect to various other forms of administrative routine. So it doesn't compare equally to the Western term of art, which is just with respect to combat operations, but it is also not a full change over of permanency within command. I hope that came out clear the way I explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you properly, we're talking about the relevant period, so we're talking about July 1995. The rules provide that with resubordination, the soldier or the unit which participates in a crime is responsible to the command or the officer to whom it is resubordinated. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is how the VRS chose to delineate that particular responsibility. It would be the responsibility of the command that had received that unit and whose subordination they were under at the time to initiate the actions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude, based on that, that the commander of the units, that is sending a part of its manpower to the resubordinated would be responsible up until the moment those soldiers came under the jurisdiction of the superiors of the unit to whom they are being resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. And again the practical application that we see of that with respect to many of the actions of the military prosecutor is a situation where before charges can be filed or investigations can be started against various soldiers, the effort is made to find out under whose command they were at the time the offence occurred. If, for example - and again using this as nothing more than a hypothetical example - if a unit or if soldiers from the Bratunac Brigade which had been subordinated or resubordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps committed a number of criminal acts in that area and then returned to Bratunac, the process would be that it would be the responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, whom they were under at the time of the commission of the acts, to initiate proceedings. So hopefully that example -- and again, it's completely hypothetical with respect to players, underscores the idea that I'm trying to get across.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely Mr. Butler. I just want to ask you: Would you agree with me that resubordination, because of the requirements of the combat operations in the VRS, was something that happened quite frequently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were frequent occurrences of being transferred from the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps to the IB Corps or the Sarajevo Corps, so because of a lack of manpower the situation was that resubordination was something that was resorted to quite frequently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would just like to ask you to help us with the term "resubordination." Could we clarify the following situation. I will try hypothetically, using hypothetical examples in order to make it clear to me and everyone else here. So could you please try to answer the questions that I will put to you first. First we have the following hypothetical situation: Parts of the Zvornik Brigade are participating in the Krivaja 95 operation. I assume that you know that this was actually the practical situation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic, is given a task. He forms, I would call it, an ad hoc unit and goes to execute his task to the area of the Srebrenica safe area. Amongst others, he takes two members of the engineering company with him. They're pioneers, as they're called, or people who are qualified for demining activities. In the Krivaja 95 operations in the area of Srebrenica, one of the members of the engineering company commits a war crime. Who does he belong to as a soldier? Who is his commander? Who needs to report the act? And who is supposed to punish him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular respect, and given the fact that while the units of the Zvornik Brigade are involved in Krivaja 95, that they did not resubordinate under the command of the Bratunac Brigade, the soldier to whichever battle group that he particularly belonged to or directly to the command element of the ad hoc unit which was created and then from there to its commander, which would be Pandurevic in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there any situation in this relationship that such a unit would be directly accountable to the Drina Corps, because it was moved from the zone of operational activities of the Zvornik Brigade and was transferred to the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that given the physical presence of the brigade commander, first of all; and second, as a Drina Corps unit it would always be under the general jurisdiction of the Drina Corps. The fact that Pandurevic is leading the unit means that it goes through him. I do not believe that you can say that because they're operating out of the brigade zone, even though the brigade commander is present, that because he's out of his zone he would not have that command function and responsibility. So the chain of command exists, it just existed in a different location than the normal zone. If, for example, to look at the other side of this hypothetical, if the battle group in question had not been led by the brigade commander or members of the staff and in fact had been placed directly subordinate to the Drina Corps IKM or to, perhaps, another brigade to reinforce them, then you would have a situation where perhaps the brigade commander is not involved and it would be a different brigade commander or directly to the command and staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we then agree that in this hypothetical situation, a crime committed by a member of the engineering company is not something that the commander of the engineering company would ever be held responsible for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object at this point. Hypotheticals for general background -- to give us an idea of general background questions, I'm not objecting to. But if we're getting very specific, in order for it to be relevant it should reflect facts that the counsel anticipates coming into the record or that have already been in the record so that it has some relevance to what we're doing. I'm not aware of any facts that are relevant regarding the pioneers committing any crimes. As a general hypothetical to give us a broad picture, I have no objection. But now we're getting into deeper hypotheticals that really didn't exist. I think one did exist that counsel may be getting to, but at this point I'm objecting any further going into this hypothetical for relevancy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that objection is quite relevant. Mr. Stojanovic, you have to show a specific case rather than give some very general, hypothetical questions to this witness, otherwise we'll get no where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I shall now refer to 46.4 of the indictment and I will move to a specific situation. This was just a background for the question I am about to put and I will refrain from further hypothetical questions; there is no need for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let's go back to more specific issues. A second situation in which I would like you to talk about resubordination and I'm asking for your opinion is the following: An officer of the Main Staff comes to the command of the Zvornik Brigade and asks to use an engineering unit. The way he asks is for -- the equipment of the Zvornik Brigade engineers should be sent to the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Brigade. Who's supposed to approve such a move? Who is it in the system who is to approve for this engineer or for that unit to go to the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Brigade? And I apologise for using the term "zone of responsibility." I know how disputable it is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming that we're talking about an officer on the Main Staff who is in fact in the engineering branch and within his competence to do so, and again assuming that it has gone through the next level of command which is the Drina Corps, given that you have the physical movement of brigade troops and resources from one unit to another unit, this is something that would have to be cleared through by the brigade commander. It is something that would involve him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. This was an answer that I expected; that's why I laid a hypothetical background. And another thing about subordination. The units of the civilian protection, their command, can they be subordinated or resubordinated to the army or, alternatively, do they work according to their authorities and coordinate their activities with the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is the latter. They work according to their authorities which are a part under the auspices of the Ministry of Defence, they coordinate their activities with the army. There may be times when they can be physically subordinated to units of the army, but again that is not something that the army itself can manifest. That direction would have to come from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. So the Ministry of Defence of the Republika Srpska is the one that can order the use of civilian protection and coordination of the units of the civilian protection with the army. And it is never a brigade commander or the commander of any other tactical unit. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably if the brigade commander needed to use the civilian protection assets, the permission to actually use them may be delegated down to the Ministry of Defence office in that specific municipality, but it is certainly something that has to at least go through the Ministry of Defence chain of approval. It is not an independent act that that brigade commander can do on his own.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably have. It may have been a while. I believe -- let me take a moment here to just kind of scan through it. Okay, sir, I believe I'm familiar with this statement. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a statement by a member of the engineers; his name is mentioned on the list that you have analysed and who -- that we are going to look at today. This is the person which is mentioned in one part of the indictment against Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have been told that maybe if I mention the name of this witness, although he's not a protected witness, that if -- maybe we should go into private session if the Prosecution wants us to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Just for a second I think if we could go into private session, I think we can clear up the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And thank you to my learned friends. So I can use the name of the witness, so I will use P178.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can you please comment on what you see on page 8, line 20 of this witness's statement, that is, the English version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters have this statement in B/C/S as well, so I believe we will be able to follow this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the relevant part that I would like to ask you something about. So the question was where he was on the 14th. He says: "On Friday morning, Major Jokic told me to get ready, together with a truck, to report to the civilian protection in Zvornik. I didn't know where I was headed for. I reported to the civilian protection when I prepared the truck and they told me to wait. I was in the lorry, and after noon, we left for Bratunac. Together with me, there were Rajko Djokic from the civilian protection and Dragan Mirkovic and Arsen Krunic. Those people worked in the civilian protection." And then the investigator asks him to repeat the names and he repeats the names and says at the end: "Once we started," and he refers to these people, "the told me that we were on our way to Bratunac, and that we would stay there for 15 to 20 days to clean Srebrenica. Srebrenica was very dirty." Could you follow this part? Could you -- did you find it could you read it, and could you and follow it, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct. I was able to track it and I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So these questions are relative to the situation that we have just discussed. This is a member on the engineering unit and he's talking about being sent by Jokic to the civilian protection in Zvornik. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He spends about half a day there, and after that together with three other members of the civilian protection from Zvornik, he leaves for Bratunac to execute a task which consisted of the clean-up operation of Srebrenica. This is the task he was given by the people who were in his company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a task that he was given by the civil protection people, yes, sir. Whether or not -- I mean, I have to assume that the task was cleared through the engineer company, although it doesn't specify in this part of the interview. But I mean, I think it's a fair assumption that the task was cleared through the engineer company, particularly if it was going to be 15 to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We shall come to that and we shall see whether the documents of the engineer's company did back up such an activity. But let's not waste time reading this document. This member of the engineering arrives in Bratunac, does not receive any task, stays at the Hotel Fontana on the night between Friday and Saturday. Then on Saturday from members of the civilian protection of Bratunac, he is escorted by a member of the civilian protection from Bratunac. He goes to the Kravica warehouse and he receives a task to transport bodies of the killed civilians from the Kravica warehouse to the mass grave in Glogova. My question to you, Mr. Butler, is as follows: In view of what you have told us about resubordination, who does this soldier belong to on the 15th of July when he finds himself in the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance -- again, probably the most conservative way to look at it would be that he would have been detached from his company in Zvornik and attached or resubordinated to the civilian protection people and would still be under their direction, leading to these tasks at the Kravica warehouse. So I think that's probably, again, the most conservative way to look at that. I mean, again given the fact -- at least with respect to this particular individual, the function that he's being asked to do, at least from his respect, is not criminal in nature. Again, his responsibility would be to -- the fact that he was attached to the civilian protection regiment -- or, I'm sorry, probably on the civilian protection organisation, not regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, on arrival in Bratunac and on receiving his orders from the civilian protection in Bratunac, from that moment on he is subordinated to them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how it would work with respect to he was detached from his company in Zvornik, the engineer company, and then put at the disposal of the civilian protection people in Zvornik. They sent him down pursuant to a task in Bratunac. I don't know enough about the organs of the civilian protection with respect to how they exercise control of their people to be able to make an observation as to whether he's working for the civilian protection people in Zvornik down in Bratunac or whether he's working directly for the civilian protection people in Bratunac. But I am comfortable saying that while he's conducting this particular activity, he's certainly not under the direct command of the engineer company in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Mr. Butler. Does that mean then that in legal terms according to the rules of the Army of Republika Srpska he should be processed if he had participated in the war crimes by those that he was resubordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that, again primarily because I don't know enough about the civilian protection organisation with respect to how that works. Whether the civilian protection organisation would go through the armed forces or whether they would request that the parent unit take legal action, I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether at any point in time somebody from the civilian protection of Bratunac or Srebrenica informed the commander of the Zvornik Brigade that this particular soldier of the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade participated in any sort of crime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Just one more thing to clarify. If I understood you well, the arrival in the zone of responsibility of a different brigade or by a soldier of the Zvornik Brigade and a piece of equipment of the Zvornik Brigade implies that the commander has been informed and has approved that; I'm talking about the brigade commander here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular case, the implication is both the commander of the brigade which is detached that soldier or equipment and if it's resubordinated to the other brigade the implication that the receiving commander is aware of that fact as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that the commander of the engineers according to the rule is not authorised, does not have the authority, to send one of his soldiers together with equipment to the zone of responsibility of a different brigade if his commander is not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree. I don't think that the engineer company commander would be able to do that unless he were doing it pursuant to the orders of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a clarification there. It's not clear if we're talking about the chief of engineering or commander of the engineering company, and that of course is an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next question. I have put my question precisely in the way it was answered. I asked about the commander of the engineers company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Am I right in assuming that not even the chief of the engineering company can do something like that without a prior approval of the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe that's a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I would like to go back to one segment of the indictment, since we are talking about item 46.4 of the indictment where my client is charged with being in command [as interpreted] of this soldier of the engineers company and that he was the one in charge of the removal and burial of the bodies in the Kravica warehouse. In such a situation, Mr. Butler, can we talk about the chief of engineers being in a position to plan such an activity if the event indeed happened in the way portrayed by this particular witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the statement by this individual witness, the witness indicates - and I'm at page 8, line 20 of the English language translation - that he was ordered by Major Jokic to - with his truck - to go to and report to civilian defence in Zvornik. The witness, at least to my knowledge in this particular part, does not indicate whether or not Major Jokic had an advanced knowledge of where this individual would be going and what he would be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Sinatra, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is a problem with the transcript and it's a very important one to the defence of Mr. Jokic. On line 22, 16.09.57, it says: "My client is charged with being in command of the soldier." And Mr. Stojanovic never said "command", he said "under the direction." And it's a very important distinction in the record. So I would like for the record to reflect that we need to make that correction before we go any further, because command and direction are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. And just to further clarify it, the indictment -- that's what the indictment says, that this soldier was under the direction of Mr. Jokic. There's not this talk about him being in command and planning the operation. That's not there and it's not in the indictment, and I know we have sometimes translation issues which is why I had spoken earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Ms. Sinatra, I think you made a very good point, but you have to bear in mind that I can only deal with one counsel to this witness. So if you have some problems, just pass it over to the lead counsel and I think we will make that correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was just such a very important piece of technical transcription, and Mr. Stojanovic can't see the monitor at the time I'm viewing it. But also I do want to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention that when Mr. Viada from Spain was cross-examining, Ms. Issa was allowed to assist him at the same time on the Prosecution's team. I just ask for equal treatment for the Defence team as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends what kind of issue, whether it's a procedural issue or a substantive issue. Here we come across a substantive issue, so I hope that one counsel should deal with one witness at a time. But if there's a procedural issue, you may raise your suggestions and comments on this part. Whether it's a substantive or procedural can be decided by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: I would like to bring to the attention that Mr. Stojanovic's doesn't read English so he doesn't know what the translation is coming up. And reflecting -- and I would like to ask the Trial Chamber's permission during this cross-examination to assist in any way that I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course you could but the best way is to maybe put it down on a piece of paper and pass it to your interpreter and to Mr. Stojanovic. But anyway, your intervention has got a point. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we have interrupted Mr. Butler, if I'm not mistaken. So let me just resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you started talking about page 8, line 20, and this witness says that Major Jokic ordered him. And then you said: I don't know whether Major Jokic knew anything in advance about all this, and apologise, I'm just paraphrasing what you said before we interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. The statement, or at least this segment of it, does not indicate that Major Jokic instructed the witness in this case why he was going down to Kravica and what the purpose was. So again, not knowing that, it's hard to infer criminal or other intent behind it. I mean, again most conservatively, at a point in time the command of the Zvornik Brigade was instructed to send individuals down for -- to begin the clean-up operation at the Kravica warehouse or to assist in the operation. It would not presumably have been necessary as a component of that for anyone who initiated the order from Bratunac or from the Drina Corps or from the Main Staff to have explained in detail to the Zvornik Brigade why they needed the individual and what the greater context of it, whether it was a criminal act or a legitimate act or something of that nature. So like I said, there are a lot of facts, that obviously I don't know associated with this, but there certainly -- the interpretation that there's nothing intrinsically incorrect or unlawful about at this point what Major Jokic is asking this particular individual or directing him to do and who to report to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We will continue on to prove exactly where Major Jokic sent him, and this witness will probably tell us that, but we wanted to hear from you that in all of these actions there is nothing criminal in any of them. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I am mistaken, but it is the time for a break now or are we planning to take a break at 4.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we are going to take a break at 4.30, but if you like we could break now and have an early start.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We say tie the horse where the aga tells you, so I am completely in the Court's hands. I can either wait until after the break or I can move on to the next topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's sit ten minutes more. We'll break at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I would just like to at least start on a new topic which I think could be very interesting, and that is the command of the engineering company. And I would just like the usher to help us to show the witness Exhibit D26 and D41, and then we can comment on them together. Mr. Butler, could we first look at Exhibit D26/3. These are -- and this is Rule 24, company and then engineering platoon.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have me at a bit of a disadvantage. The versions which I have do not have the exhibit number on them, so I'm just -- let me put it on the ELMO and you'll tell me, I assume, if it's the right document. This particular one, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. You're right. That's the one. You did not include this exhibit in your analysis, but the Defence used it already when it was examining Mr. Obrenovic. So it has its ID number, and that's D26/3, but I just want to ask you if we can try to comment on this, Article 25. What commands the engineering company, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the engineering company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So in this controversial period, in July 1995, did the Zvornik Brigade have an engineering company or platoon in its composition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They did have an engineering company in its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I think that during the examination-in-chief, you said that this engineering company numbered approximately 90 men. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us a little bit about the structure of the Zvornik Brigade Engineering Company, how many platoons did it have and what were they called?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was organised into three platoons. One, I believe, was a pioneer platoon; the other was a general engineering construction platoon; and I believe the third platoon was heavy equipment and road building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And these three platoons, did they have their commanders in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There were designated platoon commanders for each platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in view of their training and education, were these platoon commanders able to carry out the tasks and duties of platoon commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The education and training of both the company commander at the time and the platoon commanders were certainly not up to what the JNA would have envisioned for its officers under those circumstances. In many cases, and I believe probably an excellent example is in the case of the company commander, they were civil engineers, some of who had very limited military background -- or in some cases with the platoon commanders, civilian construction workers, who because of their technical training were placed in those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I wanted to ask you. Would you agree with me that two platoons of the engineering company - so we're calling it the road-building platoon and this one -- you called it general engineering and construction and this other one for heavy equipment and road building, by their structures don't they imply the know-how of people who are involved in construction, road building, and things like that; whereas, the pioneering platoon which is involved in laying down mines, demining, and so on is one that is more dealing with strictly military tasks and requires more of military know-how in order to do that. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other two functions are also military tasks, so I think it's just a question of focus. All three functions are military-related functions. All three, ideally you would have experienced individuals. And certainly in the case of the Zvornik Brigade at that time, the level of experienced officers who could have performed that function would not be what a commander would obviously like to have. They were doing the best that they could under the circumstances, like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But we agreed that they were all people who were qualified for construction equipment and construction activities. So as civilians, they had undergone training to carry out such tasks. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a fair assumption, sir, yes. I can't say that as a fact, I don't know, but I agree it's a fair assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to go back to this Article 25 we have in front of us, Mr. Butler. You said a company is under the command of a company commander. You also used the daily orders book or logbook of the engineering company. Isn't that so, you used that in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that the daily order logbook of the commander of the engineering platoon is a book of commanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it reflects the daily orders which were given either by the engineering company commander or in his name. I'm not sure what you mean by the phrase "is a book of commanding." So maybe there's, again, a linguistic issue that could get some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just noticed we're getting to the break, and since we're going so long it would be nice to have a full break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always agree with what the Court says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll have our break. We'll resume at 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, please continue. We'll sit until 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we left it off with the question about the command document. What does such a document imply? I'll try and clarify. I believe we are on the same page; however, if you remember when we were talking about control and command or directing and the command, we said that command is carried out through instruction, command, order, and directive, and here we have a book or a log of commands issued. Am I right when I say that this is one aspect of documents used within the process of commanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that respect, sir, yes, this particular book reflects the commands and orders that have been given. That is correct. So I believe we are on the same sheet of paper again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. In that sense, I put my question to you. I said that in view of the fact that companies commanded by the company command and that his command are issued through orders and that this is what this book is all about, the logbook of command orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They reflect the orders and the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Kindly look at the Defence exhibit under number 41/3. We are talking about Article 21 of this book of rules. I assume that you have already seen this and that you have already analysed this in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't believe we have the specific 1974 book. I've read it over at the break, of course. But the roles and responsibilities of the company platoon commander are not inconsistent with other regulations that we have with that respect. So even though I say I haven't seen it until recently, I can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just in brief outlines. If I understand you well, Article 21 of these combat rules says that a platoon commander is in command of a platoon and then Article 21 also lists the duties of the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Line 5, duties of the company commander, it says that the commander is the person who organises and implements the participation, and then it lists the types of combat activities and defence activities. Then line 6: Organises and controls the implementation of all the orders issued and other measures of security prescribed. Then the next line, it says: He controls the replenishment status of his company with all the materiel and equipment. And then the last line: Controls the execution of tasks, provides his subordinates with necessary assistance, and informs. Am I right in saying that all of these are duties of a company commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So according to the rules he is the one in command, who organises the work of the company, who controls the implementation of orders, he is one who controls the way these tasks were carried out, whether they were carried out in a proper manner, and he is also the one who provides his subordinates with the necessary assistance in the implementation of tasks and orders. Am I right in assuming all this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect to his -- the direct command of his company, all of this is as listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that at that time the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade had a deputy commander who was also the commanders' existent for morale and religious matters. He was a member of that company as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was one individual acting as the deputy commander in the absence of the commander. I don't know that at the company level there was a formalised position as a commander's assistant for morale matters. I thought -- I think that was a little low with respect to where you find those positions. I could be mistaken, but I think we're talking about the same individual certainly functioning as the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So what we have to agree on is the fact that at the time there was a person who discharged the duties of the deputy commander and who replaced the commander in his absence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I would kindly ask the usher to show -- to show you a part of the transcript from the trial which took place on the 10th of October when Obrenovic testified. So can this be put in front of you so that you could provide us with some comments on this. Kindly look at the first page at 11.31.19, can you please, 11.31.19. Can you please start reading from that line. At that moment, a question was put by the Chamber and the witness answered: "The commander of the engineers in July 1995 was Dragan Jevtic. He had all the authorities and all the rights regulated by the rules which were then in effect. He could command the unit. He could issue orders. In more simple terms, he could issue tasks. At that time in July 1995, the chief of engineers was Major Dragan Jokic. His position in the service was not a command position. He was more like an advisory body. Looking from that perspective, he was in the position to issue orders or to distribute tasks. He could only provide professional advice." And now we come to a paragraph that I would like you to comment and help us with. "However, according to a previous order issued by Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic, and in view of the complexity of the tasks that had to be carried out by the engineers' company and because the commanders of that company were not professionals and were not qualified in the field, the commander authorised the chief of engineers to command the engineering unit, which he did from time to time." Within the context of this part of Obrenovic's testimony, I would like to ask you a few questions. During your investigation, sir, did you come across a document, a written exhibit that would prove that this statement is correct? Have you come across a document proving that there indeed was a transfer of command from the superior commander to the subordinate commander in this matter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing in writing to my knowledge with respect to a transfer of command order which Colonel Pandurevic places Major Jokic in command of the engineer company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the system of decision-making in such a serious matter, could one expect that authorities were transferred from one company commander to another company commander or to another officer -- should be issued in a written form?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about an actual transfer of command, yes, sir, it would be in a written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree that the commander of the engineering unit should be aware of something like that, that some of his authorities are taken away from him by a certain decision if indeed there was a decision of that kind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be something that the company commander would be aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the usher's assistance again. Can you put Exhibit Number D47/1 and D40/3 and D47/2/3, those are two statements given by the commander of the engineering company when the OTP were carrying their investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, kindly look at the English version, page 57, line 26, in the statement given by this particular witness to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you ready for my questions concerning this statement, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Butler, you were present when the commander of the engineering unit gave this statement. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and read this part of the statement which is relevant, and then I'll ask for your comment. Mr. McCloskey asks the question: "Did you ever, meaning you the commander of the company, sign the bottom of this book where the company commanders are mentioned." And the witness says: "It is possible." Then: "And what does that mean when you sign that bottom of the orders, when you sign this page?" And the answer: "It means basically that the order from the brigade was forwarded and those are daily orders, what is being planned for that particular day." "Q. So it is just an acknowledgment of the commander's orders? "A. Yes. I don't understand, which commander? "Q. That would be Mr. Jokic, wouldn't it? "Witness: Yes, yes. That's it. "Q. Or maybe Obrenovic? "A. Command of the brigade, because Jokic just passed it on because Jokic couldn't issue orders." If what the commander of the engineering unit is put in the context of what you were talking about a little while ago, and that is that if authorities were being taken away from the commander of the engineers' unit, he should be aware of that. Would you then agree with me that it is right to conclude that this simply did not exist, there is -- there was no authorities being taken away and there was no authorities being passed on to somebody else. You said that there was no written order to that effect and that the commander of the engineering unit should be basically aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. From this -- this passage -- this comment from Mr. Jevtic reflecting that his understanding of the responsibility of the engineer staff officer and the fact that you do -- you have a situation, there's certainly no written order which might reflect that the command competences of an engineer company -- of the engineer company commander were somehow limited, I agree with your preposition on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may conclude, thank you Mr. Butler. This part of Obrenovic's testimony was not corroborated by anything that you came across during your investigation in terms of any material evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly with respect to documents, nothing in the orders or things of that nature. With respect to some other material, again it was the general view that because of the lack of military experience that -- of the commander's, be it the company commander or the platoon commanders, that the expectation was that the engineer staff officer would have an additional burden with respect to making sure that orders from the brigade being transmitted down to the engineer company were as precise and as simple and as appropriately detailed as possible, knowing that once those orders were received at the company level, they would do their best to carry them out without having a long -- or a military background, so to speak. Those are an increased emphasis on the roles of the staff officer. Those are not abrogations of the company commander's own right to command. So in that respect while Major Jokic is expected to play perhaps a greater role in engineering-related functions in detailing the commander's requirements down to the company, again from these two pieces of information, it's not an abrogation or a limitation on the authorities or the responsibility of the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, it has never been the objective of this Defence to say that the chief of engineers is not duty-bound to transfer authorities. Yes, he is a professional who can do that. But it has been our objective to say that there is no written order to the effect of authorities being taken away from the commander of the company and given to the chief of engineers. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree. I have not come across any document which would reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. And let's bring this to an end. Have you ever during investigation come across any written order by which Jokic issues any order to the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The scope of the focus with respect to me and what we were doing is generally in the July time frame. I can't say that of the roughly 15.000 Zvornik documents that we have, that I've gone back over prior points in time just to look for something like that. It may exist, it may not. I just don't know that I can give you a valid answer for that. I haven't seen it but, outside of the July time frame, I haven't been looking for it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Now, I would like to go back to Exhibit Number 47, item 1, again the testimony of this same witness. And let's look at page 75, line 26. The first statement, page 75, line 26 of the English version, please. Let's confirm what we have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read the passage which I think is important, Your Honours, on page 75, line 26. Again, the same interview with the commander of the engineering unit, and the Prosecution asks: "Okay. So if the 15 of you were in the field on the 13th, meaning the 13th of July, 1995, how many of the 60 remaining were out in the field on the 13th?" The witness says: "I don't know. But I know when the 15 of us lived in the company, there were maybe three or four persons left behind." "Who were they? "Slavko Bogicevic. I know that he stayed the time because he was the assistant commander for morale and he was practically my replacement. "Q. Who else? "A. There were two or three other men and so on and so forth." And then the next answer, page 76, line 12: "No, Slavko remains there as the deputy of the company commander. I'm not sure who else stayed. "Q. How old was he? "A. Who, Slavko? He was about 50. "Q. What experience does he have in operating heavy construction machinery and supervising construction works? "A. Slavko was a member of the engineering unit before I joined. He is a mechanical engineer by trade. "Q. Could he run a large-scale operation in order to dig up a number of holes? "A. I don't know." Can we agree, Mr. Butler, judging by this paragraph from the statement that at that time the commander of the engineers who was not there at the time, he had a deputy and that the deputy was the person who is mentioned in this paragraph? Can we agree on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I, therefore, conclude, given what you said about single officers, that there is always one officer present when commands are being issued about the unity of command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what -- I understand the question. There's always one officer present? I mean, in a physical sense -- can you rephrase the question perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. My understanding is that commanding means that the chain of command is not interrupted. There must always be someone who is in command, who issues commands. So the unity of command means that there is always one person who is in command. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's within that context that I want to ask you this question: We have a company commander, when he isn't present, when he isn't physically present we have a deputy company commander. One of the officers is always present in the company. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly someone within the chain of command is always going to be present. I believe in this case the individual in question is functioning as the deputy commander. I mean, he is an officer in that respect. I'm not sure what his actual rank is. But within the context that you mean this, that is correct. There is always going to be somebody in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my question. Could you just have a look at this addition to the statement of the company commander. This is Exhibit 47.2/3. It's a conversation between the Prosecution and the company commander dated the 17th -- the 11th of July, 2002. And at one point the Prosecutor asks the witness, I think it's on page 2. He asks the witness whether he remembered -- the Prosecutor asked the witness whether he remembered telling them that Bogicevic was responsible for burials. The witness replied, yes, when he wasn't in the company, Bogicevic was in charge. And then the witness further stated that Bogicevic on that day came with him 11th of July, 2002. He went with him to Banja Luka and they spoke with him about the matter, but that he is not sure whether Bogicevic would be prepared to tell the Prosecutor everything. Have you found the place where this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is just a continuation of what we spoke about a minute ago, if the company commander is not present, in such cases his deputy takes over and replaces him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this appears to be -- we've gone over this before, they're just using prior testimony or information reports not to question or impeach or refresh the recollection of the witness, but to establish factual points, and that is not -- that's not proper cross-examination. He hasn't asked Mr. Butler any relevant questions related to that. So I would object to the use of this material in such a way. It's just -- we're going to just -- reading it over and saying: Is that right. And he's saying yes. And then we go on to the next one. I mean, there's a lot of witnesses out there. We could be here for a long time. They're supposed to bring these folks in. Though, on the other hand, I may be able to save some time that Mr. Jokic is not charged with being a commander and it is the understanding of the Prosecution that Mr. Bogicevic was the deputy commander who was in command while Mr. Jevtic was in the field during these critical days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand there is no dispute on those facts between the parties. Mr. Stojanovic, maybe the best way is you put a question to this witness first, then you can show the documents in your hands to impeach this witness. Maybe this is the best way. I understand you have tried to identify a kind of chain of command which may be relevant to this case. You may move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm aware of the fact that my client has never been charged with being in a command position, but I'd just like to remind you that we're basing ourselves on the testimony of Dragan Obrenovic in response to a question by Judge Vassylenko. That's what we're basing ourselves on and on the statements and the documents and the testimony of witnesses, we have confirmed this. I won't ask any more questions about this. I will ask Mr. Butler another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said I turn to 47/2/3, but I have no other questions about it. Thank you. I would now like to move on to another field which I think is of great importance for the defence of my client that has to do with the duties of the duty officer and the presence of officers from the Zvornik Brigade and brigade command on the 14th and on the 15th. Could you have a look at the transcript from the hearing of the 11th of November. D43/3 is the number of the document. Mr. Butler, could you have a look at line 21 of the transcript when you answered Mr. McCloskey's question about the duties of the duty officer. "Most of the duties that the duty officer receives require that he informs the commander of them, because this requires a commander's decision or the decision of the chief of staff. But this means that the duty officer," and this is what I want to ask you about. If the commander and the chief of staff for any reason are not accessible - and we will discuss this matter - are not accessible or it's not possible to establish contact with them or you can't establish contact with them, the duty officer, according to the rules, has the authority to take over the initiative and issue the orders that are essential in accordance with the combat situation at the time. That was your answer. So I wanted to ask you a few questions about this. Could we have a look at Exhibit P394. That's a rule that's called instructions on the work of the command and staff. Is that correct, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And here you referred to Article 65 and Article 66 of these regulations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just show me when it is stated in the regulations that the duty officer can, as you said, take over the initiative and issue essential orders in these two cases if he is not available and if communication cannot be established.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is covered, in my opinion, by this first bullet here, which is essentially to receive and dispatch orders and reports when other organs are resting or when ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, could we read this. In Article 66 it says: "The duties of the duty officer include receiving and dispatching orders and reports when other organs are resting or when ordered to do so." It doesn't state that he can take over the initiative and issue orders. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't explicitly state that -- or does not, let me make sure that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I then draw the conclusion that this opinion of yours is based on your interpretation of this decision?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is based on this as well as the practical applications of the duty officer position that is reflected in other documents. But with respect to this alone, yes, this is my interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the rules do not state that he can issue orders, but interpreting this in a broad sense, this is the conclusion you came to with regard to those two cases when we're speaking about the commander not being available and it being impossible to establish communication. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The position as defined leaves open the possibility, at least with respect to my interpretation of it, that when critical orders have been passed down from the superior command, if the commander or chief of staff are not in the position to give the required orders, that the duty officer as, in effect, the commander's representative is in power to do so. That is why if one examines the duty officer rosters of the brigades, it makes it clear that the position is only held by those people who are considered to be superior commanding officers in deference to the fact that they may need to make these decisions and should be experienced people to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you're saying that this is the case if the commander isn't present or is not available or there is no telephone line that can be established to speak to the commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be either the commander or the deputy commander, or even if you were to take it one step further by position, the chief of operations, who in the absence of the commander or deputy commander would fill in as the acting deputy commander. If in a position where all three of those are either not available or because of the military situation are outside of the means of communication, it would be the duty officer who would be expected to take over and pass or give the orders that would be required under the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have understood you, Mr. Butler, but I just want you to confirm that this is your interpretation and not something that is contained in the regulations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. In this respect, it's not explicitly contained in Article 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This new exhibit might help us to understand what the duties of the commander are. I would like to ask the usher to take our exhibit, D57. This is the military encyclopedia dated from 1969 which provides the definition of the duty officer. It's from the military encyclopedia. It's very brief. I'd just like to read through it. "The duty officer is the most senior organ of internal service within a unit, command, institution, military compound barracks, and is directly subordinated to the unit commander that positions him and on whose behalf he issues the necessary orders and directs the activities of the internal service and he maintains order in the unit. His duty lasts for 24 hours." Can you help us to understand what this means in the senior organ of internal service, what does this mean, internal service in a brigade command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, when we're talking about the internal services of a brigade command, that would be the operations section, that would also include perhaps the rear services and morale personnel, those types of general issues. I think that's what we're referring to in this respect within the internal services of a unit or command if we try and translate this to brigade. It's a very generic description. So I think that's what we would be referring to in this context. The operational related services of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For us, the organ of general service means the lowest level of service, the purpose of which is to provide services for the brigade command - and through our expert we will discuss this matter in greater detail. But the essence of the issue is that your interpretation of the provisions of Article 66 is also based only on the fact that this occurs when the commander is not available or when it's not possible to speak to the commander over the phone. In the course of your investigations, did you ever come to the conclusion that the commander of the Zvornik Brigade or his deputy at the time, on the 14th, the 15th, and the 16th, were not available and were not in a position to perform their duties as commanders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Alternatively the brigade commander and the brigade deputy commander were performing their duties. They were in, if not always physical contact, certainly radio communications with the duty operations section and the duty officer or his representative during the period from the 14th through -- or even before that, the period of the 13th through the 17th. So in that context the deputy commander and commander were always available with respect to the issuance of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I think that all further questions are superfluous now. I know we are not charged with command responsibility, but for the sake of the Trial Chamber I wanted to demonstrate the position of Dragan Jokic as a duty officer. I wanted to demonstrate what that position actually was. This is why I want to go through what we have prepared with you. Have you analysed the presence of Dragan Obrenovic in the command of the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: His physical presence I assume which you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've agreed that the -- there's always the possibility of communication, but I wanted to clear up the matter of his physical presence. On the 14th and 15th, up until that time -- the 14th and the 15th and the morning of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have analysed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what conclusions did you come to, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD JOHN BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly there is differences -- I mean, first of all, with respect to documents or intercepts, there is nothing that leads me to conclude his physical presence. I am aware that not only Mr. Jokic but at least one other witness has stated that on the 14th that Major Obrenovic was present for at least some periods of time in the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. It may be actually two other witnesses as well. On the 15th I believe that then Major Obrenovic acknowledges his presence with respect to the meeting that occurred approximately noon on the 15th with Mr. Vasic and then later Colonel Pandurevic arriving back from the Zepa battlefield. And that would include individuals from the MUP and from -- specifically Colonel Borovcanin, Milos Stupar, Vasic was there, Obrenovic was there, and then Pandurevic was there at various times within that about one hour time frame. So again, with respect to the 14th, there is conflicting information. With respect to the 15th, I think most of the witness accounts are fairly consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I'll try to say this as directly as possible, because I think your joint objective is to establish the truth. Our Defence claims that Dragan Obrenovic was in the command of the Zvornik Brigade in the morning on the 14th of July.
